kurals.tamil:
கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும்
இரவாமை கோடி உறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karavaadhu uvandheeyum kannannaar kannum
iravaamai koadi urum.
kurals.meaning: Even when there are people as dear as one's own eyes who would gladly give without hiding anything, not asking them at all is worth ten million times more.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your kindest aunt would happily give you anything you asked for. The Kural says it is still far better, and makes you stronger, to manage on your own and not ask, even from someone that kind.
kurals.university: The chapter Iravaccham (இரவச்சம், 'dread of begging') deliberately answers the preceding chapter Iravu (ch. 106), which permitted asking only of fitting, generous givers; here Valluvar raises the ideal higher, so that even such givers should not be asked. Karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealing') and uvandhu eeyum (உவந்தீயும், 'who give with delight') describe the best possible donor, and kannannaar (கண்ணன்னார், 'those like one's eyes') marks them as most precious; the hyperbole koadi urum ('attains a crore', i.e. ten-million-fold good) is the commentators' measure of the superiority of not asking. In the line of interpretation that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, the point is that dignity (maanam) lies in enduring want rather than in depending even on a willing friend. Pope renders it 'Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live, / Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu teach that everything that depends on others brings pain, while everything that depends on oneself brings happiness, and call this the short definition of pain and pleasure.
hinduism.explanation: Manu's householder code makes self-reliance the very definition of happiness and dependence the definition of pain.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle so strictly that even a loving, willing giver should not be leaned on.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of Bühler's rendering and not re-verified on a live page this session; a strong thematic fit on self-dependence, though Manu does not specify the generous giver.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.”
christianity.explanation: Paul reminds the Ephesian elders that, though the churches would gladly have supported him, he provided for himself with his own hands.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul declines to depend even on friends who were willing to give.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a strong parallel, since Paul refuses support from willing believers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever abstains from asking others, Allah will make him contented, and whoever tries to make himself self-sufficient, Allah will make him self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: After giving to the Ansar until nothing was left, the Prophet told them that refraining from asking brings contentment and self-sufficiency.
islam.tie_back: The hadith matches the Kural closely: the Prophet was himself a generous giver, yet he urged people not to ask even of him.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; near one-to-one, since the setting is a generous giver who still commends not asking.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Grace after Meals, the traditional text asks God not to make the worshipper dependent on the gifts or loans of flesh and blood, but only on God's own full and open hand, so that one may never be put to shame.
judaism.explanation: Jewish liturgy turns the wish never to depend on human gifts into a daily prayer.
judaism.tie_back: The prayer, like the Kural, treats dependence on even well-meaning human givers as something to be avoided.
judaism.source: Birkat HaMazon, third blessing (traditional siddur text) (paraphrase)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known liturgical line, not re-verified against a specific live translation this session; a close thematic fit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what is the bliss of debtlessness? There is the case where the son of a good family owes no debt, great or small, to anyone at all.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that owing nothing to anyone is one of a householder's four kinds of bliss.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of asking no one, however kind, matches the Buddha's bliss of being beholden to no one.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; debt is not the same as begging, but the shared ideal of being beholden to no one is clear.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Living without begging from friends, strong in affection and who are like the apple of our eyes, who withhold not their assistance from us, is life indeed.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrains on the dread of mendicity call life without begging, even from loving and generous friends, the only true life.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural itself: friends 'like the apple of our eyes' who 'withhold not' are exactly the kannannaar who give without concealing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture, used because its chapter on the same theme is a near one-to-one match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “There is nothing worse than being always ways on the tramp; still, when men have once got low down in the world they will go through a great deal on behalf of their miserable bellies.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, thanks Eumaeus for sparing him from going about the town to beg.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the hero who must play the beggar calls a life of going about to ask the worst there is, which is the Kural's dread.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified on classics.mit.edu, where the text reads 'always ways' as printed; it speaks of vagrancy in general, not of refusing willing givers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And he is the sort of man to confer benefits, but he is ashamed of receiving them; for the one is the mark of a superior, the other of an inferior.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's great-souled man is happy to give but ashamed to receive, because receiving puts him in a lower position.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shares the instinct that receiving, even from a willing benefactor, lowers one's standing.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong fit, though Aristotle's motive is status and honour, while the Kural's is dignity under need.

kurals.tamil:
இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின் பரந்து
கெடுக உலகியற்றி யான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Irandhum uyirvaazhdhal vendin parandhu
keduka ulagiyatri yaan.
kurals.meaning: If the one who shaped the world meant some people to live by begging, then let that maker himself wander about like a beggar and perish.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a game where the rules say some players must beg the others just to stay in. You would say the rules are unfair and the person who made them should try playing that way himself. That is how angry the Kural is that anyone should have to beg to live.
kurals.university: This is one of the boldest couplets in the Kural: Valluvar curses ulagiyatriyaan (உலகியற்றியான், 'he who fashioned the world') with the very fate of the beggar, parandhu keduga ('may he wander and perish'). Commentators in the tradition that follows Parimelazhagar read it as a conditional imprecation: if the creator had ordained begging as a means of life, he deserves to wander as beggars do; the force is ethical outrage that anyone should be reduced to irandhum ('even by begging') staying alive. Modern glosses differ in emphasis: Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the creator literal, while Kalaignar Karunanidhi's gloss pointedly says 'the one said to have created this world', distancing the verse from theism, and scholars have debated whether ulagiyatriyaan means a god, fate (ul), or the human order that permits destitution. Pope renders it 'If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go, / Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Beholding superior and well-behaved and modest persons persecuted, while the sinful are happy, I am sorely troubled. Beholding this thy distress and the prosperity of Suyodhana, I do not speak highly of the Great Ordainer who suffereth such inequality!”
hinduism.explanation: In exile, Draupadi openly reproaches the Ordainer for letting the virtuous suffer while the wicked prosper.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Draupadi dares to blame the world's maker for an unjust distribution of fortune.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section XXX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong parallel in reproaching the creator, though Draupadi's complaint concerns injustice generally rather than begging.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded crieth out: yet God layeth not folly to them.”
christianity.explanation: Job complains that God seems to ignore the cries of the poor and oppressed.
christianity.tie_back: Job, like the Kural, questions a creator who lets people be reduced to misery.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; Job protests rather than curses, so the tone is milder than the Kural's.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when it is said to them, ‘Spend from that which Allāh has provided for you,’ those who disbelieve say to those who believe, ‘Should we feed one whom, if Allāh had willed, He would have fed? You are not but in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who blame God's will for others' hunger as an excuse not to feed them.
islam.tie_back: Islam rejects blaming God for poverty, so this is a contrast: where the Kural curses the maker, the Qur'an places the duty on those who could feed the poor.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; included as a next-best match, because Islamic theology does not permit the Kural's imprecation against the creator.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Far be it from You to do such a thing, to bring death upon the innocent as well as the guilty, so that innocent and guilty fare alike. Far be it from You! Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?”
judaism.explanation: Abraham challenges God directly, holding the Judge of all the earth to his own standard of justice.
judaism.tie_back: Abraham, like Valluvar, holds the maker of the world to account for unjust suffering.
judaism.source: Genesis 18:25 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; the boldness of challenging God matches, but the subject is collective punishment, not begging.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhuridatta Jataka, the Bodhisatta argues that if Brahma were truly lord and maker of the whole world, he would not have ordered it so full of misery and injustice, so the creator is either powerless or unjust.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka uses the suffering of beings as an argument against a just, all-powerful creator.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'if the maker willed begging' runs on the same logic: a world that forces people to beg indicts whoever made it.
buddhism.source: Bhuridatta Jataka (Jataka No. 543, tr. E. B. Cowell et al.) (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the Cowell translation, not verified on a live page this session; the logic is closely parallel.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though Lakshmî withdraw from them and God be angry, the excellent will not stand with bended neck before the ignorant who bury their money in the earth.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil quatrains say that the noble will not bow to beg from hoarders even if fortune leaves them and heaven turns hostile.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defies whatever higher power might force a person to beg, though it defies by endurance rather than by cursing.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; Jain doctrine denies a world-creator, so the Kural's premise does not fit Jainism, and this Tamil Jain verse is a partial match on defiance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the gods keep hidden from men the means of life. Else you would easily do work enough in a day to supply you for a full year even without working.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that Zeus in anger hid the easy means of life from mortals, so that people must struggle for their bread.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like the Kural, traces human want back to the will of the powers who ordered the world.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 42-44 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; Hesiod explains rather than condemns the gods' decree, so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lactantius reports the argument attributed to Epicurus: God either wishes to take away evils and cannot, or can and does not wish to, or neither wishes nor is able; if he both wishes and is able, where do evils come from and why does he not remove them?
philosophy.explanation: The classical problem of evil asks how a good and powerful maker could allow suffering.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural puts the same dilemma as a curse: a maker who wills that people beg cannot be both just and worthy.
philosophy.source: Lactantius, On the Anger of God 13 (argument attributed to Epicurus) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified on a live page this session; the dilemma is general rather than about begging.

kurals.tamil:
இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்துதீர் வாமென்னும்
வன்மையின் வன்பாட்ட தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmai idumbai irandhudheer vaamennum
vanmaiyin vanpaatta thil.
kurals.meaning: There is no harder-hearted folly than the bold notion that the misery of poverty can be cured by begging instead of by effort.
kurals.elementary: If your bike breaks, you could keep asking friends to lend you theirs, or you could learn to fix your own. The Kural says choosing to ask forever instead of fixing things yourself is the worst choice of all.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on vanmai (வன்மை), 'hardness, toughness, boldness': the 'toughness' of deciding inmai idumbai (இன்மை இடும்பை, 'the affliction of want') will be ended by asking (irandhu theervaam) is called harder than any hardness (vanmaiyin vanpaattadhu il). Following Parimelazhagar's line, Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar supply the implied contrast with effort (muyarchi): the fault is abandoning work and choosing to live by others' gifts. Solomon Pappaiah adds the parenthesis '(without working it off)', and Pope's explanation speaks of remedying poverty 'by begging (rather than by working)'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say, / 'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to perform his prescribed work, because action is better than inaction and even the maintenance of the body cannot be achieved without work.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita holds that no one can live, even physically, without doing one's own work.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle: the remedy for want is one's own work, not living off others.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not re-verified this session; the Gita speaks of duty-bound action rather than begging specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he and his companions worked night and day so as not to live off anyone's bread.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul treats working, not relying on others' bread, as the answer to need.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a strong fit on effort as the alternative to dependence.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is better for anyone of you to take a rope (and cut) and bring a bundle of wood (from the forest) over his back and sell it and Allah will save his face (from the Hell-Fire) because of that, rather than to ask the people who may give him or not.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that even hauling firewood to sell is better than asking people for help.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact contrast: remove poverty by honest labour, however humble, not by begging.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; near one-to-one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And anyone who does not need to take [charity] and yet takes, will not depart from this world before he actually needs [charity] from others.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah warns that whoever takes charity without real need will end up truly needing it.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah, like the Kural, condemns choosing to live by others' gifts instead of one's own means.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 8:9 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the Sefaria API; a strong fit, though the Mishnah addresses unnecessary taking rather than the choice not to work.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha lists the dangers of idleness, such as refusing to work because it is too cold, too hot, too early or too late, so that new wealth is not earned and existing wealth runs out.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns lay people that excuses for not working lead to poverty.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's target is the same: the person who gives up effort and expects poverty to be solved some other way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; it concerns idleness, not begging as such.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Since it is a means of removing the affliction of poverty for one to beg for himself, then let affliction be my portion, and let precious wealth depart from me.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet would rather keep his poverty than remove it by begging.
jainism.tie_back: This answers the Kural's very phrase inmai idumbai irandhu theervaam: the noble refuse to cure the affliction of want by asking.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 6 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (first sentence of the stanza); a Tamil Jain text, near one-to-one in wording.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work the work which the gods ordained for men, lest in bitter anguish of spirit you with your wife and children seek your livelihood amongst your neighbours, and they do not heed you.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses to work, or he will end up begging from neighbours who will stop listening.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like the Kural, rejects begging as a remedy for want and insists on work.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 397-400 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near-direct parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon's Memorabilia, Socrates advises Aristarchus, whose house is full of destitute kinswomen, to set them to useful work such as making clothes, and the household is soon both fed and happier.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates' answer to a household's poverty is productive work, not dependence or borrowing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise insists that want should be met by effort, not by asking.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; a good thematic fit on work as the cure for want.

kurals.tamil:
இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளாத் தகைத்தே இடமில்லாக்
காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Idamellaam kollaath thakaiththe idamillaak
kaalum iravollaach chaalbu.
kurals.meaning: The nobility that will not agree to beg even when one has nothing to live on is so great that the whole world cannot contain it.
kurals.elementary: Think of someone who has almost nothing but still won't ask for handouts, because they want to stand on their own feet. The Kural says that kind of courage is so big that even the whole world isn't big enough to hold it.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pun on idam (இடம்): idamillaak kaalum means 'even when there is no means (of life)', while idamellaam kollaa means 'which all the room (of the world) cannot hold'. The quality praised is saalbu (சால்பு, 'nobility, fullness of character', the same root as saanraanmai, ch. 99), here specified as iravu ollaa, 'not consenting to beg'. In the line of commentary that follows Parimelazhagar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take the second half as 'even when one is destitute' and the first as 'a greatness not equalled by all the worlds together'. Pope renders it 'Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worth / Has excellence of greatness that transcends the earth.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the poor Brahmin Sudama visits his childhood friend Krishna, now a king, but out of self-respect does not ask him for anything; Krishna honours him and grants him prosperity unasked.
hinduism.explanation: Sudama's refusal to beg even from a willing, divine friend is celebrated as true greatness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story praises a destitute man who will not ask even when he has nothing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known narrative, not verified on a live page this session; a strong narrative fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to work with their own hands so that they live honourably and depend on no one.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's dignity of not depending on others is the same aim Paul sets for the Thessalonians.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text (margin: 'or, of no man'); a reasonable fit on honourable self-support, though the verse does not address extreme destitution.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises poor people whose restraint is so great that others mistake them for well off.
islam.tie_back: These are exactly the Kural's people: destitute, yet unwilling to beg.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; near one-to-one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And anyone who needs to take and does not take, will not die of old age until he supports others with his own money. Concerning him the verse says: ‘Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord and whose hope is the Lord’ (Jeremiah 17:7).”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah blesses the needy person who refrains from taking charity and promises that he will one day support others.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah, like the Kural, honours the person who will not ask even in real need.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 8:9 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the Sefaria API; near one-to-one on refusing to take despite need.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk who does not despise what he has received, even though it be little, who is pure in livelihood and unremitting in effort — him even the gods praise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk who is content with little and pure in how he lives.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it gives cosmic praise to someone who keeps his dignity with very little.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; Buddhist monks live on alms, so the parallel is contentment and purity of livelihood, not refusal to beg.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is it, therefore, a reproach to a man if he starve and keep his integrity inviolate, rather than fill his stomach by the disgraceful practice of mendicity?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet asks whether there is any shame in starving with one's integrity whole rather than eating by begging.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's idamillaak kaalum iravollaa saalbu: refusing to beg even when there is nothing to eat.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 2 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text, near one-to-one in thought.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that no work is shameful; only idleness, which leads to want and begging, is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's nobility likewise counts poverty without begging as honourable.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days l. 311 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match, since Hesiod praises work rather than the refusal to beg in destitution.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant teaches that a person has a duty of self-respect and should not become anyone's lackey or let others trample on his rights with impunity, because servility betrays one's own dignity as a rational being.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, abasing oneself before others violates a duty owed to the humanity in oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's saalbu, refusing to beg even in want, is a form of the self-respect Kant calls a duty.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, The Metaphysics of Morals, Doctrine of Virtue, on servility (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; Kant's subject is servility generally rather than begging.

kurals.tamil:
தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை ஆயினும் தாள்தந்தது
உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினிய தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thenneer adupurkai aayinum thaaldhandhadhu
unnalin oonginiya thil.
kurals.meaning: Even if it is only gruel so thin it looks like clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what your own effort has earned.
kurals.elementary: A sandwich you made yourself, even a plain one, can taste better than a fancy one someone handed you. The Kural says food you earned with your own work is the sweetest food of all.
kurals.university: Thenneer (தெண்ணீர், 'clear water') describes the gruel: adupurkai (அடுபுற்கை, 'cooked porridge', taken by Puliyur Kesikan as gruel of coarse grass-grain, pullarisi) so watery it looks like clear water. Thaal thandhadhu (தாள்தந்தது, literally 'what the foot/effort gave') is glossed by commentators following Parimelazhagar as what is brought by lawful effort (muyarchi); Puliyur Kesikan adds 'by effort joined with right conduct'. Oonginiyadhu il means 'there is nothing sweeter beyond it'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is sweeter than to taste the toil-won cheer, / Though mess of pottage as tasteless as the water clear.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man who cooketh in his own house, on the fifth or the sixth part of the day, with scanty vegetables, but who is not in debt and who stirreth not from home, is truly happy.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked by the Yaksha who is truly happy, Yudhishthira names the man who eats poor food at home but owes nothing to anyone.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds the greatest happiness in a meagre meal that is one's own.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section CCCXI (Yaksha's questions) (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; near one-to-one: scanty food, independence and happiness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm promises happiness to the one who eats the fruit of his own labour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds sweetness in food earned by one's own effort.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a strong fit, though the psalm does not stress how plain the food is.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands. The Prophet (ﷺ) of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says no food is better than food earned by one's own hands.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim nearly word for word: nothing is sweeter than eating what one's effort has earned.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; near one-to-one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who benefits from his hard labor is greater than a God-fearing person … while with regard to one who benefits from his hard work, it is written: ‘By the labor of your hands you will live; you are happy and it is good for you’ (Psalms 128:2).”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud ranks a person who lives from his own labour above one who is merely God-fearing.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud, like the Kural, puts the joy of living from one's own effort at the top.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified via the Sefaria API; the ellipsis omits Steinsaltz's explanatory gloss, and the passage praises labour rather than plain food as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the son of a good family has wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. When he thinks, ‘I have wealth earned through my efforts & enterprise ...’ he experiences bliss, he experiences joy.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the joy of having honestly earned wealth one of the householder's kinds of bliss.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta finds a special sweetness in what one's own effort has gained.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (internal ellipsis marks a repeated phrase); a strong fit, though it speaks of wealth, not poor food.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga's account of Mahavira's ascetic years describes him living on rough food such as rice, pounded jujube and beans, accepting whatever plain fare came to him without craving for better.
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture holds up Mahavira's contentment with coarse food as a model of freedom from desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also finds even the thinnest gruel sweet; the Jain stress is on non-attachment rather than on earning it.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; Jain monks live on alms, so this fits the plainness of food but not the Kural's praise of earning it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon serve disguised gods a humble meal of garden herbs, a little bacon, olives, cheese and eggs in plain earthenware, offered gladly from their own small store.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their meagre but honest meal, shared freely, is the most praised feast in the Metamorphoses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's thin gruel, their humble food is made precious by being their own.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; the story praises hospitality more than self-earned food.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says that plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet once the pain of want is removed, and that bread and water give the highest pleasure when brought to hungry lips.
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus argues that simple food fully satisfies and that self-sufficiency is a great good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shares the claim that the plainest food can be the sweetest, though it ties the sweetness to effort.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (in Diogenes Laertius X, tr. R. D. Hicks) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the live text could not be retrieved this session; a good fit on plain food, without the Kural's emphasis on earning.

kurals.tamil:
ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும் நாவிற்கு
இரவின் இளிவந்த தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aavirku neerendru irappinum naavirku
iravin ilivandha thil.
kurals.meaning: Even if you are only begging water for a thirsty cow, nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you need to ask a stranger for water, not even for yourself but for a thirsty animal. The Kural says that even then, asking feels hard and lowering, which shows how heavy begging is.
kurals.university: The couplet chooses the most innocent possible request: aavirku neer (ஆவிற்கு நீர், 'water for a cow'), a deed of dharma, since caring for cattle was held highly meritorious. Puliyur Kesikan, following the Parimelazhagar line, adds that the cow is dying of thirst and the request is made out of compassion; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'asking out of regard for dharma'. Even so, naavirku iravin ilivandhadhu il, 'for the tongue there is nothing more debasing than begging'. The figure is an a fortiori argument: if even this is lowering, begging for oneself is far worse. Pope renders it 'E'en if a draught of water for a cow you ask, / Nought's so distasteful to the tongue as beggar's task.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Indian tradition often recalls that when Vishnu went to King Bali to beg for land, he had to take the form of Vamana, a dwarf, and the story is commonly read as showing that even God is made small by asking.
hinduism.explanation: The Vamana avatara is popularly cited to show how asking diminishes even the highest being.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's point is the same: asking lowers the asker even when the cause is good.
hinduism.source: Vamana and Bali (Bhagavata Purana 8.18-22) with the traditional reading of it (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the moral that 'begging makes even Vishnu a dwarf' is traditional interpretation rather than the Purana's own statement.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable, the dismissed steward says he is too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg.
christianity.tie_back: The steward's shame at begging shows the same sense of degradation the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; the shame matches, though the steward is not a model of virtue.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man keeps on asking others for something till he comes on the Day of Resurrection without any piece of flesh on his face.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that habitual begging strips away a person's face, that is, his honour.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith says asking disgraces the one who asks.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the hadith targets habitual begging, while the Kural stresses even a single, well-meant request.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records the counsel to make one's Sabbath like a weekday rather than become dependent on other people.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching says it is better to give up even the honour due to the Sabbath than to ask others for help.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, avoiding the need to ask is placed above even a religious good.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known saying, not verified on a live page this session; a close structural parallel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kasibharadvaja Sutta, the Buddha refuses food offered to him after he has recited verses, saying that what is gained by reciting verses is not fit for him to eat.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha will not accept food that has been earned by what looks like asking or performing for it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows sensitivity to how a request, even a dignified one, can taint what is received.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; the Buddha lives on alms, so this is a partial parallel about improper gain rather than begging.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Is the gently walking in the way of asceticism more grievous than the saying to others, Give me at least something, thus debasing one's dignity of the custom of doing homage to others, to whom he has attached himself by making their acquaintance?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says even the hard ascetic path is easier than debasing oneself by saying 'give me something'.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that nothing degrades the tongue more than the words of asking.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 9 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text with a strong fit on the degradation of asking, though without the Kural's cow.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own hall, has to go round the suitors asking each for a scrap and endures their mockery and blows to carry out his plan.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the hero, begging for a just purpose, is shown suffering the humiliation that begging brings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a good cause does not remove the indignity of asking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a narrative parallel to begging for a good end, not a direct statement about the tongue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that nothing costs so dear as what is bought with prayers, and that the words 'I ask' are heavy and painful to say, so a good benefactor should spare people the need to ask.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the act of asking as itself painful and humiliating to the one who asks.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified on a live page this session; a close match on the pain of uttering a request.

kurals.tamil:
இரப்பன் இரப்பாரை எல்லாம் இரப்பின்
கரப்பார் இரவன்மின் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Irappan irappaarai ellaam irappin
karappaar iravanmin endru.
kurals.meaning: I beg all who beg this one thing: if you must ask, do not ask of those who hide what they have.
kurals.elementary: If you ever really need help, ask someone with a kind and open heart, not someone who pretends to have nothing. The poet even says 'please' to everyone who has to ask for help, because he cares about them.
kurals.university: The couplet is a striking play on one verb, irattal ('to beg'): irappan ('I beg') irappaarai ellaam ('all beggars') irappin ('if you beg') karappaar iravanmin ('do not beg of concealers'). Valluvar thus makes himself a petitioner on behalf of petitioners, a rhetorical humility the commentators note. Karappaar (கரப்பார், 'those who conceal') recalls karappu in ch. 106 and 1061's karavaadhu; the advice, in the line following Parimelazhagar as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, is that a person forced to ask should at least avoid those who hide what they have. Pope renders it 'One thing I beg of beggars all, 'If beg ye may, / Of those who hide their wealth, beg not, I pray'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad's parting instruction to students says that gifts should be given with faith and not without faith, with generosity, with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats a grudging or faithless gift as defective giving.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'concealers' are exactly the grudging givers the Upanishad rejects, and it warns askers away from them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; it addresses the giver, not advice to the asker.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns against taking food from a stingy host whose heart is not in the giving.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice: do not seek from those who give with a hidden, unwilling heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a near-direct parallel.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who are stingy and enjoin upon [other] people stinginess and conceal what Allāh has given them of His bounty - and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment -”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who conceal the bounty God has given them.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an's 'concealers' match the Kural's karappaar, the very people askers are told to avoid.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong on concealment, though it condemns the concealer rather than advising the asker.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who desires that he himself should not give and that others too should not give: he is a wicked man.”
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot sorts givers into four types and calls the one who neither gives nor wants others to give wicked.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's karappaar belong to this worst type, so the asker should not turn to them.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:13 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the Sefaria API; it classifies givers rather than advising askers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets the miser against the wise man who delights in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tells askers to go only to the open-handed, never to the miser the Dhammapada condemns.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the contrast of miser and giver fits, but there is no advice to askers.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Will the excellent then go for alms to any others but to those who will embrace them and say, Come to my house and eat?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says that the noble, if they must ask, go only to those who welcome them warmly.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice in positive form: ask only of the open-hearted, never of concealers.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 3 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text closely matching the Kural's counsel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod contrasts the free-handed and the close-fisted and advises dealing with the generous.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod separates open givers from tight-fisted ones and steers people towards the former.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 354-355 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair parallel, though Hesiod's maxim concerns reciprocity rather than begging.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca observes that a benefit given slowly and grudgingly, after the asker has been kept waiting, loses its value, since the giver who hesitates has long been unwilling.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats reluctant, hidden unwillingness as spoiling a gift.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's karappaar give, if at all, in just this spirit, so askers should avoid them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; Seneca addresses givers, not askers.

kurals.tamil:
இரவென்னும் ஏமாப்பில் தோணி கரவென்னும்
பார்தாக்கப் பக்கு விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iravennum emaappil thoni karavennum
paardhaakkap pakku vidum.
kurals.meaning: Begging is an unprotected little boat; when it strikes the rock of refusal, it splits apart.
kurals.elementary: Picture a small paper boat floating on a stream. It looks fine until it bumps into a hard rock and breaks. Asking for help is like that boat, and someone's cold 'no' is the rock that breaks it.
kurals.university: The couplet is an extended metaphor (uruvakam): iravu ('begging') is a thoni (தோணி, 'small boat, raft') that is emaappil (ஏமாப்பில், 'without protection, unsafe'), and karavu (கரவு, 'concealment, refusal') is a paar (பார், 'submerged rock, reef'); when it strikes, it pakku vidum ('splits open'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as in Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, supply the implied sea: the boat is taken to cross the ocean of poverty. Kalaignar Karunanidhi reads the rock as 'the stone heart that hides what it has and says no'. Pope renders it 'The fragile bark of beggary / Wrecked on denial's rock will lie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda hymn on liberality says that the riches of the generous never waste away, while the one who will not give finds no one to comfort him.
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn contrasts the lasting wealth of the giver with the friendlessness of the refuser.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows the other side of that refusal: the asker's fragile hope breaks on it.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not re-verified this session; it concerns the refuser's fate rather than the wrecking of the asker's hope.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
christianity.explanation: James condemns those who send the needy away with words instead of help.
christianity.tie_back: Such a refusal is the 'rock' on which the Kural's small boat of asking breaks.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a good fit on refusal, without the Kural's image.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that those who withhold God's bounty will be burdened with it on the Last Day.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's karavu, withholding, is the same fault, here seen from the side of the one who is refused.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it targets the withholder's fate rather than the asker's ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The pauper speaks in terms of mercy; / The rich person’s answer is harsh.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the poor plead gently while the rich answer them harshly.
judaism.tie_back: The poor man's plea and the rich man's hard reply are the Kural's frail boat and its rock.
judaism.source: Proverbs 18:23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; a close match on the fragile plea meeting a hard response.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Parabhava Sutta lists among the causes of a person's downfall having much wealth, gold and food and yet enjoying it alone, and failing to support those who depend on one.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names solitary, ungenerous enjoyment of wealth as a road to ruin.
buddhism.tie_back: The rich man who hides his wealth is the 'rock' of the Kural, and the Buddha says he wrecks himself as well.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; it concerns the miser's downfall, not the asker's.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Will those who possess clear understanding follow after such men as constantly revile them, saying, These poor men will become rich through our means; they cannot acquire wealth of themselves?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet asks whether the wise will run after patrons who mock and despise those who depend on them.
jainism.tie_back: Such scornful patrons are the hard rock on which the Kural's frail boat of asking breaks, so the wise do not set out on it.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text that fits the hard-hearted patron but lacks the Kural's image of shipwreck.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, asks the suitor Antinous for food; Antinous refuses, insults him, and strikes him with a footstool, while the other suitors had at least given him something.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous' violent refusal of a beggar is the Odyssey's emblem of a hard heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar's request breaks on Antinous' refusal just as the Kural's boat breaks on the rock.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a strong narrative parallel to begging meeting hard refusal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He once begged alms of a statue, and, when asked why he did so, replied, ‘To get practice in being refused.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic trained himself to bear refusal by begging from a statue.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes knew what the Kural knows: begging is fragile and refusal is the rock that breaks it, so he hardened himself against it.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks, via Wikisource)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource; Diogenes accepts begging and trains against refusal, while the Kural rejects begging, so the fit is in the shared view of refusal.

kurals.tamil:
இரவுள்ள உள்ளம் உருகும் கரவுள்ள
உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iravulla ullam urugum karavulla
ulladhooum indrik kedum.
kurals.meaning: The heart melts at the thought of begging; at the thought of those who hide what they have and refuse, even that melting heart is destroyed.
kurals.elementary: When you see someone who has to ask for help, your heart feels soft and sad. But when you think of someone who has plenty and still says 'I have nothing', your heart feels crushed. The Kural describes both feelings.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two thoughts side by side: iravu ulla (இரவுள்ள, 'when one thinks of begging') the ullam urugum ('heart melts'); karavu ulla ('when one thinks of concealment/refusal') ulladhooum ('even what there is', i.e. the melting heart itself) indrik kedum ('perishes, ceasing to exist'). The pun on ulla ('to think') and ullam ('heart') and ulladhu ('what exists') is characteristic. In the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah, the speaker's compassion for beggars is overwhelmed by horror at those who refuse while having plenty. Pope renders it 'The heart will melt away at thought of beggary, / With thought of stern repulse 'twill perish utterly.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita, Krishna says that those who cook food only for their own enjoyment, without first offering and sharing it, eat nothing but sin.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita condemns keeping one's food for oneself as sinful.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's horror at those who hide what they have reflects the same judgment on selfish keeping.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not re-verified this session; the verse is about sacrificial sharing, a partial fit for refusal to the needy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John asks how anyone who closes his heart to a needy brother can have the love of God in him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's melting heart and the heart 'shut up' against the needy are the two sides John sets against each other.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the bolls.life KJV text; a strong fit on compassion against a closed heart.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are - those invited to spend in the cause of Allāh - but among you are those who withhold [out of greed]. And whoever withholds only withholds [benefit] from himself.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that those who withhold out of greed only harm themselves.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's karavu, greedy withholding, is condemned here as self-destructive.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it condemns withholding without the Kural's emotional contrast.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If, however, there is a needy person among you, one of your kindred in any of your settlements in the land that the ETERNAL your God is giving you, do not harden your heart and shut your hand against your needy kindred.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids hardening one's heart and closing one's hand against a needy person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's melting heart is what the Torah demands, and the hard, concealing heart is what it forbids.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:7 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; the edition prints ETERNAL in small capitals; a strong fit on the hard heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the miser is to be overcome by generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural's heart is crushed by the concealer, the Dhammapada offers generosity as the answer to him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best match that addresses the miser but not the melting heart.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Since one's mind melts with angnish when one reflects on a life of mendicity, what must their feelings be who receive alms!”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says even the thought of begging melts the mind with anguish, so the actual experience must be far worse.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: the heart melts at the very thought of begging.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on wisdomlib.org, quoted as printed including the misprint 'angnish' (anguish); a Tamil Jain text matching the Kural's first line but not its second.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Erysichthon cuts down Ceres' sacred oak and refuses all pity; he is punished with a hunger that consumes his wealth, makes him sell his own daughter, and finally drives him to devour himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The pitiless, grasping man is destroyed from within by his own insatiable greed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's concealer, Erysichthon's hardness ends in his own utter ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; a next-best match on pitiless greed and self-destruction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith opens The Theory of Moral Sentiments by arguing that however selfish people may be, there are principles in human nature that make them care about the fortune of others, so that we feel sorrow at the sight of misery.
philosophy.explanation: Smith grounds morality in the natural sympathy we feel for those in distress.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's heart that melts at begging is Smith's sympathy, and the concealer is the one in whom it has died.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; it matches the first half of the Kural only.

kurals.tamil:
கரப்பவர்க்கு யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ இரப்பவர்
சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karappavarkku yaangolikkum kollo irappavar
sollaadap pooom uyir.
kurals.meaning: The beggar's life leaves him the moment he hears 'no'; where, then, does the life of the one who says it hide itself?
kurals.elementary: When someone asks for help and hears a cold 'no', it can feel like all their hope has gone. The Kural wonders how the person who said 'no' while having plenty can keep living so easily, as if their heart has gone into hiding.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with a bitter rhetorical question built on a pun: karappavarkku yaangu olikkum kollo ('where does it hide for the concealers?'), the 'it' being uyir ('life'), which in the second line pooom ('goes away', with lengthening for metre) from the irappavar ('askers') as soon as the word of refusal is spoken (sollaada, 'when the word is uttered'). Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line, as given by Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar, read it as amazement: since the refusal kills the asker, the refuser's own life ought to depart too, so where does it hide? Pope renders it 'E'en as he asks, the shamefaced asker dies; / Where shall his spirit hide who help denies?' and paraphrases that the very word that kills the beggar should also kill the refuser. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A widely quoted verse of the Mahabharata and Puranas says that when a guest leaves a house with his hope broken, he leaves his sins to the householder and takes away the householder's merit.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu householder ethics hold that turning away a hopeful guest robs the householder of his own spiritual life.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the refusal that crushes the asker should rebound on the one who refuses.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, and Vishnu Purana 3.9, verse on the disappointed guest (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse; the exact section numbering in Ganguli was not verified this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that whoever shuts his ears to the poor will one day cry out and not be heard.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs expects the refuser's own life to pay for the refusal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong fit on the refuser's fate.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who withholds and considers himself free of need / And denies the best [reward], / We will ease him toward difficulty. / And what will his wealth avail him when he falls?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient will be eased towards hardship, and his wealth will not save him.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks where the refuser's life can hide; the Qur'an answers that his wealth will not shelter him.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote markers omitted); a good fit on the refuser's eventual ruin.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that anyone who averts his eyes from giving charity is regarded as though he were worshipping idols.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching treats refusing charity as one of the gravest sins.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's amazement that the refuser's life does not depart fits this view of refusal as near-idolatry.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known saying, not verified on a live page this session; a strong fit on the gravity of refusal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Vasala Sutta says that whoever, when a brahmin or ascetic comes at mealtime, does not offer food but scolds him instead, is to be known as a true outcast.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines the outcast as someone who refuses and insults a person asking for food.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's refuser, whose 'no' kills the asker, is the Buddha's true outcast.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; a fair fit on condemning harsh refusal.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a person being tormented with poverty, rejecting true wisdom and allowing ignorance to abide in his mind, goes to a person and says, Give me alms, and if the person so asked refuse to give, will he not die from very shame at that moment?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain Tamil poet says that a poor man who asks and is refused dies of shame on the spot.
jainism.tie_back: This is the second line of the Kural: the asker's life departs at the word of refusal.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 31 (Dread of mendicity), stanza 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a Tamil Jain text matching the asker's death at refusal, without the Kural's question about the refuser.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as weary travellers, are turned away from a thousand homes; only the poor couple Baucis and Philemon take them in, and the gods then drown the whole neighbourhood that refused them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The households that shut their doors on needy strangers are destroyed, while the generous poor are saved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid answers the Kural's question: the refusers' lives cannot hide forever.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on a live page this session; a strong narrative fit on punishment for refusing those who ask.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes meanness (illiberality) as falling short in giving and exceeding in taking, says it is incurable and more natural to people than prodigality, and counts it a greater evil.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the illiberal person, who will not give, has one of the most deep-rooted vices.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's refuser shows the vice Aristotle condemns.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Book IV on classics.mit.edu without exact quotation; a next-best match without the Kural's moral outrage.
